tip: Turkish says 'know how to' with a verbal noun plus bilmek: Yüzme biliyor musun is literally do you know swimming.
For 'we need to', add -memiz to the verb before gerekiyor: değiştirmemiz gerekiyor, the -miz says it is us who must.
Şemsiyemi stacks two suffixes: -m 'my' then -i 'the object', so şemsiye becomes my umbrella as the object.
A final p softens to b before a vowel suffix: mektup plus -u becomes mektubu, the object form of letter.
A vowel-final noun adds a buffer y before the object suffix: gazete plus -i becomes gazeteyi, not gazetei.
Pencereyi aç uses the bare verb stem as a command: aç = open, straight from açmak with no ending.
Insert -abil into a verb for 'can, be able': buluş plus -abil plus -iriz gives buluşabiliriz, we can meet.
Suffixes stack in order: Arkadaşlarımla is arkadaş plus -lar plural plus -ım my plus -la with, so with my friends.
A plural subject can take a singular verb: Çocuklar oynadı, the children played, needs no -lar on oynadı.
To report a command, use the verbal noun plus söylemek: içmemi söyledi means told me to drink, -mi marks my drinking.
etmek turns a noun into a verb: telefon etti means made a phone, that is, called.
A proper noun takes an apostrophe before a case suffix: İstanbul'a means to Istanbul.
A final k softens to ğ before a vowel suffix: mutfak plus -ımız becomes Mutfağımız, our kitchen.
'After' is the ablative -dan plus sonra: okuldan sonra means after school.
sayesinde means 'thanks to' and follows its noun: Teknoloji sayesinde means thanks to technology.
A relative clause comes before its noun with -düğüm: gördüğüm köpek means the dog that I saw.
The suffix -ken means 'while': beklerken means while waiting, setting the scene for the main action.
The -miş past reports something inferred or just noticed: meşhur olmuş means it has apparently become famous.
